Impiety
ĭm-pī´ē-ty
n. (want of reverence toward God; ungodliness in its active form)
Latin impietas, from in, not, and pietas, dutiful reverence — the failure of the debt a creature owes his Maker and a son his father.

Biblical Definition

Impiety is the absence of the reverence owed to God, and Scripture treats it as an act rather than a mood. Paul locates it at the head of the human case: “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom 1:18) — ungodliness first, because the offence against God precedes the offence against men. Its mark is a refusal to glorify or thank: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” (Rom 1:21). The godly man's opposite instinct is named in Hebrews: let us serve God “with reverence and godly fear” (Heb 12:28).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines impiety as ungodliness; irreverence towards the Supreme Being; contempt of the divine character and authority; an act of wickedness.

expand to see more

IMPIETY, n. Ungodliness; irreverence towards the Supreme Being; contempt of the divine character and authority; neglect of the divine precepts.

2. An act of wickedness; an act of contempt for the laws or character of God.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:18 — "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness;"

Rom 1:21 — "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened."

Heb 12:28 — "Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:"

Jud 1:15 — "To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him."

Psa 36:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David the servant of the LORD. The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes."

Modern Corruption

Irreverence is counted a small fault beside cruelty, and Romans puts ungodliness before unrighteousness in the indictment.

expand to see more

Romans 1:18 sets the order of the charge, and the order is the doctrine: ungodliness first, then unrighteousness. The modern conscience reverses it, treating cruelty to men as the real sin and irreverence toward God as a private eccentricity that harms no one. Paul's argument through the rest of the chapter is that the second follows from the first — that a race which will not glorify God or be thankful is given over, by three separate acts of judicial abandonment, to the moral collapse the chapter then catalogues. Impiety is not the harmless half of the indictment. It is the root of the other half.

Psalm 36:1 gives the anatomy: the transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes. The fear is not merely absent; it is absent before his eyes, which is to say the man has arranged his sight so that God is not in it. Romans 1:21 names the two withheld duties precisely — they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful — and both are omissions. Impiety rarely announces itself as blasphemy. It is usually a life in which God is simply not consulted, and the ingratitude of it is the part Scripture presses.

Hebrews 12:28 gives the answer, and it is not solemnity for its own sake: we receive a kingdom which cannot be moved, and therefore serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear — the reverence follows from the gift. Where reverence has to be manufactured it turns into the very superstition the Reformers fought; where the kingdom is actually received, it comes on its own, and the next clause tells why it is fitting: for our God is a consuming fire.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek asebeia (G763), ungodliness, impiety; asebes (G765), ungodly; eulabeia (G2124), godly fear, reverence; Hebrew pachad (H6343), dread, the fear of God.

expand to see more

Greek asebeia (G763) — ungodliness, impiety; Romans 1:18, 11:26, 2 Timothy 2:16, Titus 2:12, Jude 1:15, 1:18.

Greek eulabeia (G2124) — godly fear, reverence; Hebrews 5:7, 12:28.

Hebrew pachad Elohim (H6343, H430) — the fear of God; Psalm 36:1, Genesis 20:11.

Usage

"“Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” — the order of the indictment."

"“They glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” — two omissions, and the collapse that followed."

"“No fear of God before his eyes” — the sight arranged to exclude Him."
